items.title: 25.3.2 The Loss of Energy between Trophic Levels

source_refs.note: Topic 25.3.2 with the Tidbit (PDF 234-235); Figure 25.5 is replaced by an original diagram, and the energy example is given as a table.

blocks.text: There are generally three or four trophic levels in an ecosystem. Producers convert only about 1-2% of the solar energy falling on them into the chemical energy of organic matter, and only about 10% of the energy at each level passes to the next; the rest is lost at each level, so very little usable energy remains after it has passed through the organisms of the different levels.

blocks.alt: A beetle feeding on a green leaf. Three purple arrows from the beetle show where the energy of its food goes: 50% Feces, 33% Cellular respiration and 17% Growth.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.5: Utilization of energy by a heterotroph (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.5).

blocks.alt: An energy staircase. A green slab of producers (trees and grass) holds 10,000 kcal, with an arrow of energy from the Sun. Blue arrows rise to a large cube for the primary consumer (rabbit), 1,000 kcal; a smaller cube for the secondary consumer (snake), 100 kcal; and a tiny cube for the tertiary consumer (eagle), 10 kcal. A yellow Heat loss arrow leaves at each step.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.6: Energy flow in trophic levels (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 25.6).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Producers 10,000 kcal; Primary consumer 1,000 kcal; Secondary consumer 100 kcal; Tertiary consumer 10 kcal; Rabbit; Snake; Eagle; Heat loss (three times); Energy from the Sun.

blocks.title: Tidbit: short chains are efficient
blocks.text: Short food chains, with fewer trophic levels, are more energy-efficient than long ones, because energy is lost as heat at every transfer.
